question_en: If repo collateral is "on special," it most likely:
option_c: offers the highest overnight repo rate.
explanation_en: Factors affecting repo rates Collateral risk The higher the quality of collateral, the lower the rate. Collateral General collateral is the standard rate for a collateral type. demand "On special" collateral lowers the repo rate. Term The longer the term, the higher the rate. Delivery A lower rate is offered if collateral needs to be directly requirements delivered to the lender versus a third-party custodian. Financing Repo rates are affected by financing alternatives available in alternatives the market. The repo rate is the quoted interest rate on a repurchase agreement. Repo rates are generally tied to short-term interest rates and follow the central bank policy rate very closely. With the policy rate as the baseline, other factors that influence the repo rate include collateral risk, demand for collateral, term, delivery requirements, and alternative financing sources. "General collateral" refers to a broad variety (eg, maturities, coupons) of issues of the same type (eg, Treasuries, agency bonds) that serve as collateral (ie, the asset sold and repurchased) for the repo. When a certain asset, such as a specific Treasury bond, is "on special," there is great demand for that specific security to serve as collateral, which depresses the repo rate below the general collateral rate. The lender is willing to accept the lower rate in order to have that specific asset as collateral. Specialness is driven by a very specific borrowing need (eg, a short position or a futures delivery) and most often applies to a benchmark security (eg, 10-year Treasury). (Choice B) A repo to maturity is a repo with a term equal to the maturity of the underlying collateral (eg, 15 days). Special collateral is most often in great demand to satisfy a very specific obligation; however, it is highly unlikely that a repo to maturity would be able satisfy the specific collateral obligation. (Choice C) An "on special" repo will have a lower rate versus general collateral of the same term.

question_en: A large corporation based in the United States wants to borrow funds for three months as interim financing until it can complete a long-term bond issue. If the interim funding is to be unsecured, the most appropriate funding arrangement is to:
option_b: borrow directly from a bank for three months.
option_c: initiate a three-month term repurchase agreement.
explanation_en: Commercial paper is a form of short-term debt that is often used for interim financing until longer-term financing can be finalized. In addition to being short-term, commercial paper is unsecured, meaning that there is no collateral; it is only the issuer's promise to pay that backs the loan. Commercial paper is issued to multiple investors through capital markets, whereas bank loans are negotiated directly between the borrower and lender. (Choice B) Bank loans are more likely to be used by smaller corporate borrowers that do not have ready access to capital markets. Most bank loans require the borrower to secure the loan with collateral. (Choice C) In a repurchase ("repo") agreement, the borrower sells an asset while agreeing to repurchase it in the future for a predetermined price. Since the lender can sell the asset if the repurchase does not occur, a repo agreement can be viewed as a secured loan. For this reason, it is classified as a secured form of short-term debt.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.04 Fixed-Income Markets for Corporate Issuers - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following fixed-income instruments is most similar to a collateralized loan?
explanation_en: A repurchase agreement (ie, repo) is structured as two paired transactions. The first trade is a sale of securities for a specified amount of cash. At that time, the counterparties agree to a second trade in which the initial seller repurchases the securities for a slightly higher price. There is no price risk with a repo since the prices for both trades are agreed to at initiation; in effect, the price difference is interest earned on the purchase (ie, loaned) amount. The original buyer is protected from default by the securities (ie, collateral) received in the initial trade. As a result, a repo is the equivalent of a collateralized loan. (Choice A) The put provision in a putable bond does give bondholders the right to force the issuer to repurchase the bond prior to maturity, but there is no collateral (ie, no assets are pledged against the risk of default). (Choice B) An interbank loan is unsecured. In a repo, the assets purchased function as collateral.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.04 Fixed-Income Markets for Corporate Issuers - Answers.pdf
question_en: A large company with a low credit rating needs to borrow a large amount of money. If the company operates in a country with an underdeveloped bond market, which of the following is the company's most likely source of funds?
explanation_en: Bank loans are the primary source of debt financing for small- and medium-size companies. Large companies may also use bank loans instead of issuing bonds if the company: is in an underdeveloped bond market area; must compete for bond issuance in a market where government entities and financial institutions dominate ("crowd out") corporate issuers; or has a low credit rating, making bond issuance more expensive than a bank loan. A syndicated loan is made by a group (ie, syndicate) of financial institutions (eg, banks, insurance companies, and other lenders) to a single borrower. A syndicated loan is appropriate when no single lender wishes to make a bilateral loan (ie, single lender to single borrower) and take on all the credit risk of the loan (Choice A). A substantial loan to a large company with a low credit rating, as described in this case, would involve high credit risk, making a syndicate a more likely source of funds than a single lender. (Choice B) Large, established companies with high credit ratings issue bonds perceived as relatively safe investments by bond markets. For such companies, issuing bonds may be less expensive, and therefore more desirable, than taking out bank loans. The exceptions to this general rule is when bond markets are not fully developed or when government entities "crowd out" private companies in bond issuance.

question_en: Which of the following exposes a counterparty lending to a bank to the least amount of credit risk?
explanation_en: Short-term bank funding alternatives Funds deposited by individual and commercial customers Retail deposits Checking (ie, demand), savings, and money market accounts Central bank Commercial bank deposits (usually required) at central bank (reserve) funds Excess over required minimum may be lent to other banks Interbank funds Market for deposits and loans between banks Negotiable certificates Large denomination deposits with penalties for early withdrawal of deposit (CDs) Withdrawal penalty avoided by sale of deposit to another investor Repurchase Security sale paired with later repurchase of same security agreements (repos) Combined transactions equivalent to a collateralized loan A repurchase agreement (repo) is structured as a pair of transactions: At initiation securities are sold for cash, and at the same time the counterparties agree to a second trade in which the seller will repurchase those securities at maturity at a higher price. The required repurchase makes repos economically equivalent to collateralized loans. The repo buyer (ie, lender) has securities that can be sold to recover the amount owed if the repo seller (ie, borrower) fails to repurchase them. The amount borrowed in a repo is less than the value of the collateral, thus minimizing the lender's exposure to credit risk. (Choices A and C) Loans of central bank funds and negotiable certificates of deposit are not collateralized, so the lenders are exposed to more credit risk than in a repo.

question_en: When a hedge fund engages in a reverse repurchase agreement, which of the following is the most likely purpose?
option_c: Obtain securities to deliver on a short sale
explanation_en: Repurchase agreements (repos) and reverse repurchase agreements (reverse repos) have identical structures. In both transactions, the counterparties agree to an initial exchange (ie, sale) of securities for cash. The initial exchange is conditioned on the original security holder's promise to buy them back (ie, repurchase agreement). Repos are economically equivalent to a loan of cash collateralized by securities. In the repo diagram, the insurance company lending cash is not concerned with the specific security received, only that it is adequate collateral. The reverse repo has a different motivation: the hedge fund is borrowing a specific security and providing cash collateral in return. Reverse repos are often the least expensive method for borrowing securities needed to complete a short sale. A short sale is a sale of securities the seller does not own. Nonetheless, the securities must be delivered, which is the motivation for the hedge fund doing a reverse repo. Short sales may be done to speculate on declining prices or to hedge long positions. (Choice A) The hedge fund would use a repurchase agreement to earn interest since repo rates are higher than interest rates on reverse repos. (Choice B) The sale and repurchase prices in repos and reverse repos are set at transaction initiation, so neither transaction entails a direct speculation on the related security price.

question_en: The repo margin most accurately describes:
option_a: the rate of return earned by the repo lender.
option_b: the difference between the market value of the collateral and the amount loaned.
option_c: the amount of additional collateral required by the repo lender in addition to the repo
explanation_en: A repurchase agreement (ie, repo) is a type of short-term debt. It is structured as the sale of an asset, typically a high-quality, short-term bond that the seller agrees to repurchase at a future date for a specified amount. Since the terms of the agreement are known in advance, a repo can be viewed as a short-term secured loan. The repo seller is the borrower and the repo buyer is the lender. The lender is exposed to the risk that the borrower will be unable to repurchase the asset when the agreement matures. Although the buyer can sell the collateral if the seller defaults, it is possible that its market value will have declined from when the repo was initiated. To mitigate this risk, the amount loaned is less than the value of the collateral. The difference is the repo margin. In the example above, the repo margin is $1,010 − 1,000 = $10. (Choice A) The repo rate is the lender's return from the transaction (ie, the repurchase agreement's interest rate). In the example above, the price ($2 higher) that the seller pays to repurchase the asset is equivalent to the interest on the original $1,000 loan. In this case the repo rate is 0.2% for the two-month period, or 1.2% annually. (Choice C) The financial instrument that the buyer purchases is the only collateral in a repo. The repo margin is a form of credit enhancement for the loan, but it is not additional collateral.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely considered a contingency provision for a corporate bond?
option_a: The issuer's ability to call the bond prior to maturity
option_b: An increase in the bond's coupon rate if the issuer's credit rating declines
option_c: The bondholder's right to sell the bond to another investor prior to maturity
explanation_en: Typical bond contingency provisions Callability Issuer has right to redeem bond before maturity Putability Bondholder can require issuer to redeem bond before maturity Bondholder can convert bond into a predetermined number of issuer's Convertibility common shares Bonds with contingency provisions combine the cash flows of a debt security with an embedded option. Contingency provisions give either bondholders or issuers the right to take some action that alters the bond's cash flows. Exercise of call or put provisions shortens the period over which coupons are paid. In addition, calling a bond may require paying a premium over par value. Conversion of a bond may shorten the period over which coupons are paid and always results in an exchange of securities for the converted bond rather than retiring it with cash. A common contingency provision in indentures gives issuers the right to force bondholders to surrender their securities (ie, call the bond) prior to maturity. (Choice B) An increase in coupon rate due to a credit rating decline does alter a bond's cash flows, but this is not considered a contingency provision. Instead, the change in cash flows is triggered by an event specified in the indenture, not by the issuer or bondholders exercising some right. (Choice C) Bondholders generally have the right to sell their bonds to other investors in the secondary market prior to maturity, but that right is not a contingency provision since the sale would not alter the cash flows payable by the issuer.

question_en: Which of the following factors most likely impacts repo margin requirements?
option_c: Interest rates on alternative financing sources
explanation_en: Factors affecting repo margin Collateral quality The higher the quality of collateral, the lower the margin Collateral demand Lower margin is required if specific collateral is in high demand Length The longer the term of the repo, the higher the margin Counterparty risk Higher creditworthiness of counterparty, lower margin required A repurchase agreement (ie, repo) is structured as the sale of an asset, typically a high-quality bond (eg, treasury, agency) that the seller agrees to repurchase at a future date for a specified amount. Since the terms of the agreement are known in advance, a repo is a type of short-term collateralized loan. The repo seller is the borrower (ie, collateral provider) and the repo buyer (ie, cash provider) is the lender. The lender is exposed to the risk that the borrower will be unable to repurchase the asset when the agreement ends. Although the buyer can sell the collateral in the market if the seller defaults, it is possible that the market value will have declined since the repo was initiated. To mitigate this risk, the value of the collateral is greater than the amount loaned. The difference is the repo margin, which is expressed as a percentage of the value of the loan (eg, 102%, 105%). The amount of the repo margin depends upon the quality of the collateral, the demand for specific collateral, the term of the repo, and the counterparty's creditworthiness. (Choices B and C) The central bank policy rate and the interest rate on alternative sources of financing affect the repo rate, not the repo margin.

question_en: One source of funds for making interest and principal payments on nonsovereign bonds is most likely:
option_a: a special tax or fee established for that purpose.
option_b: the operating cash flows of a private corporation.
option_c: income from the loan portfolios of the supranational entity.
explanation_en: Nonsovereign government bonds (ie, nonsovereigns) are issued by government entities subordinate to national governments (eg, states, provinces, prefectures, or cities). Nonsovereigns are not normally guaranteed by the associated national government. In the U.S., these bonds are known as municipal bonds, have specific tax exemptions, and may be issued to fund specific projects like schools, bridges, or expressways. Interest and principal on such bonds are paid from the: general taxing authority of the municipality (eg, property taxes, sales taxes) revenue generated by the project funded (eg, tolls) special fees or taxes established to pay the bonds' interest and principal Since the creditworthiness and financial discipline of local government entities vary greatly, nonsovereign bonds have a range of credit ratings, and, therefore, yields; nonsovereigns guaranteed by the associated national government trade at a lower yield due to higher quality. (Choice B) Nonsovereigns are issued by governments below the national level, not by corporations. (Choice C) Funding interest and principal payments from the loan portfolio of a supranational entity describe bonds issued by a supranational organization like the World Bank or European Investment Bank.

question_en: Bonds issued by the World Bank are best described as:
explanation_en: Supranational is the designation given to bonds issued by international organizations such as the World Bank or International Monetary Fund (IMF). Such multilateral agencies issue debt to finance their activities, including fostering economic development (World Bank) and providing financial assistance to countries experiencing economic difficulties or severe trade imbalances (IMF). Supranational bonds are considered very creditworthy issues. Multilateral agencies generate strong cash flow on their portfolios of bonds and loans. These agencies' issues are further backed by the capital contributions of their member countries. (Choice A) Sovereign government bonds (ie, sovereigns) are debt securities issued by national governments. These bonds are usually backed by the issuer's full faith and credit (ie, taxing authority). Sovereigns are also creditworthy securities, depending on the size and stability of tax revenue. (Choice C) Quasi-government or agency bonds are securities issued by organizations created by national governments to perform various functions (eg, power generation/transmission, housing finance). These organizations are distinct legal entities and are often considered independent from the government. The credit quality of these securities varies widely.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.05 Fixed-Income Markets for Government Issuers - Answers.pdf
question_en: Linkers are sovereign government debt securities on which coupon and/or principal payments may be adjusted. Such adjustments are most likely linked to:
explanation_en: Investors holding bonds entitling them to receive fixed coupon and principal payments are exposed to inflation risk. To mitigate investors' risk, many governments issue inflation-linked bonds (ie, linkers). Most are based on a specified consumer price inflation index (eg, Retail Price Index in the UK). Depending on the specific sovereign issue, the inflation adjustment to cash flows could be to the coupon payments, principal amount, or both. However, linkers may not eliminate inflation risk since consumer inflation indexes may not accurately reflect changes in the price level. (Choice B) Cash flows on inflation-linked bonds are adjusted according to inflation as measured by a specified inflation index, not based on a country's GDP. (Choice C) Interbank rates (eg, LIBOR) are often used as reference rates for setting the coupon rate on floating-rate notes (FRNs). Many FRNs issued by sovereigns use interbank rates as a reference rate.

question_en: On August 8, 20X0, an investor buys a 6.4%, semiannual-paying bond with a YTM of 5.2%. The bond matures on December 15, 20X2 and pays coupon interest each June 15 and December 15. The bond trades on a 30/360 basis. If the dealer quotes a price of 102.62 per 100 of par value, the bond's flat price on August 8, 20X0 is closest to:
explanation_en: A bond's flat price is the difference between its full price and any interest that accrued since it last paid coupon interest. When selling a bond, dealers usually quote a bond's flat price as the market price. The accrued interest is added to the flat price, and the buyer pays the total amount. It should be noted that the flat price is also known as the "clean price" and that the full price is also known as the "dirty price." The exam may use any of these terms in questions related to this topic. (Choice A) 101.68 results from incorrectly assuming 102.62 is the bond's full price. Fifty-three days of interest accrued between June 15 and August 8, 20X0. The total accrued interest is (53 ÷ 180) × 3.2, or approximately 0.94 per 100 par value. Subtracting that amount from 102.62 equals 101.68. Note: The calculator keystrokes that are included with this question refer to this calculation. (Choice C) 103.56 is the bond's full price on August 8, 20X0.

question_en: A bond with 5 years to maturity has a 4.5% coupon rate and pays interest semiannually. If the bond's price per 100 par value is 97.80, the bond's YTM is closest to:
explanation_en:
The yield-to-maturity (YTM) is the discount rate used to discount a bond's expected future cash flows to estimate its present value or bond price.
The number of periods and the periodic discount rate used in the calculation depend on the frequency of cash flows. When a bond pays interest
more than once per year, the coupon payment and the number of periods are adjusted for the frequency of payments per year. Knowing the
bond's present value, face value, periodic coupon, and number of periods until maturity, solve for YTM:
Note that the calculator solution provides the periodic discount rate of 2.5%, which represents a six-month periodic rate. That rate must be
adjusted to an annual YTM of 5.0%. Due to the complexity of the calculation, a financial calculator is recommended.
(Choice A) 2.5% results from incorrectly assuming the periodic discount rate is equal to YTM, which is always quoted as an annual rate.
(Choice B) 2.7% results from using the semiannual coupon interest but neglecting to use the number of semiannual, instead of annual, periods to
reflect the semiannual payment schedule.

question_en: A bond originally issued with a 7-year maturity now has 3 years remaining to maturity. The bond has a 5% coupon rate and pays interest semiannually. If the YTM is 4%, the bond's price per 100 par value is closest to:
explanation_en: Estimating bond values Method Approach Other considerations Spot rate Value bond as a package of zero-coupon securities, discounting each by a May require adding a credit spread to risk- pricing rate reflecting the different maturities free spot rates Matrix Value bonds using the YTMs of actively traded bonds with similar coupon Need to adjust discount rate for differences pricing rates, maturities, and credit risks between bonds Many bond issues trade infrequently. As a result, a bond's most recent transaction price can be days or weeks old and may not accurately reflect its current value. Matrix pricing can be used to estimate the market price of inactively traded securities from the YTM of actively traded bonds. Securities with similar risks should have similar expected returns, so bonds that have similar credit risks, coupon rates, and times to maturity should trade at a comparable YTM. If bonds of similar maturities are not available for comparison, a market discount rate for pricing an inactively traded bond can be estimated from the yields of otherwise-similar actively traded bonds of shorter and longer maturities. (Choice A) Discounting a bond's cash flows by spot rates calculated from similar-risk bonds is an alternative to matrix pricing (not a component of it). It is another method for valuing inactively traded bonds. (Choice C) Adding a yield spread to a benchmark government bond is an alternative for estimating a discount rate, but it is not used in matrix pricing.

question_en: A bond with 4 years until maturity has a 3.5% annual-pay coupon. If the bond's price per 100 par value is 81.50, the implied market discount rate is closest to:
explanation_en: Flat price = Quoted market price For bond purchases, the quoted market price is called the bond's flat price. The amount an investor pays for the bond is the flat price plus any interest that has accrued since the bond's most recent coupon payment, since the seller is entitled to the accrued interest until the sale. The sum of the flat price and the accrued interest is the bond's full price. Interest accrues each day, so the full price increases each day. However, a bond's price is also affected by factors including changes in interest rates and the issuer's credit quality. Quoting only the flat price separates the accrued interest component (a mechanical adjustment that always increases the price) from other factors that are more relevant to investors. (Choice A) 97.40 results from mistaking the bond's quoted price of 98.24 as its full price, and then subtracting the accrued interest of 0.8375 per 100 par value from 98.24. (Choice C) 99.08 is the bond's full price after adding accrued interest of 0.8375 per 100 par value to the quoted price.

question_en: An analyst uses matrix pricing to estimate the YTM of an illiquid, 5-year corporate bond that pays a 7% annual coupon. The analyst compares two publicly traded bonds of similar credit quality, as show in the image below: Based on this data, the estimated YTM of the illiquid bond is closest to:
explanation_en: Matrix pricing is a method of estimating a bond's price or required spread when market data are not readily available, such as when valuing inactively traded bonds or determining the required yield spread when underwriting new issues. The process for using matrix pricing for inactively traded bonds (eg, debt of private firms) is as follows: First, identify actively traded bonds with the same credit rating, similar maturity, and similar coupon rate as the inactively traded bond. Then group the actively traded bonds by maturity and calculate the average yield, not the average coupon, for each maturity group. Finally, use interpolation to estimate the required market yield (and price) for the inactively traded bond (Choices B and C).

question_en: A bond that matures in four years has a 5% annual coupon rate with interest paid semiannually. If the market discount rate for the bond is 4.50%, the price of the bond per 100 of par is closest to:
explanation_en:
The price of a bond is the bond's present value: the sum of the present values of its coupon and principal (ie, par value) payments over the
remaining time to maturity. Each cash flow is discounted by the market yield to maturity (YTM), expressed as a periodic rate, over the number of
periods between the pricing date and the date each cash flow is due.
The quickest solution to the problem is obtained with a financial calculator, using the following inputs:
Number of periods (N) n × m = 4 × 2 = 8
Periodic discount rate (i) r ÷ m = 4.50% ÷ 2 = 2.25(%)
Periodic payments (PMT) (c × FV) ÷ m = (0.05 × 100) ÷ 2 = 2.5
Par value (FV) 100
c = coupon rate; FV = par value
For bonds with a compounding frequency (m) of more than once per year, the number of periods (N), coupon payments (PMT), and market
discount rate (i) must be adjusted from the given annual values to the periodic values. The market discount rate is also called the required yield or
the required rate of return.
(Choice A) 98.2075 results from using the market discount rate to determine the coupon payments and using the coupon rate to discount the
cash flows. Note that since the bond's coupon rate is greater than its yield, it is currently priced at a premium: the price must be greater than the
par value. Thus, any answer choice less than par value is incorrect.
(Choice B) 101.7938 would be the price if the bond paid coupons once per year.

explanation_en:
The price (PV) of a bond is the sum of the present value of its cash flows to maturity.
The cash flows are:
the coupon payment for each period (PMT) and
the future value (FV) at maturity (ie, par value).
The market discount rate is the required rate of return (r) (ie, market YTM).
The divisor exponents measure the number of compounding periods until each cash flows is due.
In this scenario, the bond's price can be found quickly with a financial calculator, using the following inputs:
Number of periods (N) 12
Discount rate (i) 5 (%)
Periodic payments (PMT) c × FV = (0.04 × 100) = 4
Par value (FV) 100
c = Coupon rate
For bonds that pay coupons once per year, FV, N, and the market discount rate (i) are entered as given. PMT is calculated as shown in the table
above.
(Choice A) 91.0575 results from pricing the bond as if it paid coupons semiannually (ie, PMT = 2, N = 24, i = 2.5).

question_en:
An analyst obtains the following information on a government bond:

| Bond Payment frequency Day-count convention | Data Semiannual Actual/actual |  |
|---|---|---|
| Annual coupon rate | 4.00% |  |
| YTM | 5.00% |  |
| Payment dates | 15 January, | 15 July |
| Maturity date | 15 January | 2030 |

Assuming a trade settlement date of 9 November 2020, the amount of accrued interest per 100 of par value is closest to:
explanation_en:
Bonds earn interest daily but pay interest only periodically. On the payment date, the owner of the bond receives the full coupon payment for the
preceding period. If a bond trades between coupon dates, the buyer will receive the entire coupon. Therefore, the buyer must compensate the
seller for the portion of the coupon earned (ie, accrued) since the last coupon payment.
The amount of accrued interest is determined by the par value, the coupon rate, and the period of time over which interest accrued. Several
methods, known as day-count conventions, can be used to measure that period. For many government bonds, the actual/actual method is used
as follows:
Determine the number of actual calendar days over which interest accrued (ie, days of accrued interest), starting on the last coupon
payment date and continuing to but not including the settlement date.
Determine the actual number of days in the coupon period by counting the days from the settlement date up to but not including the next
